code.t: let Split { io, fs, ffi, heap, args } = split(world);
borrow mut io as &!i in { greet(i, "cancho"); }

steps.cap: main starts with one value: all the authority there is.
split(world) hands it out once, as five separate values.
Four are not needed here, so they are released. An unused capability is still a linear value.
Only io is lent, and only to greet. greet’s signature says what it does with it.
io is released too. Nothing is left over.

code.t: let Split { io, fs, ffi, heap, args } = split(world);
borrow mut io as &!i in { greet(i, "cancho"); }

steps.cap: Same program, one release(…) left out.
fs, ffi and args are released. heap is not.
io is lent to greet as before.
heap was never consumed. A leaked capability is a leaked power, so this is an error, not a warning.

code.t: let Split { io, fs, ffi, heap, args } = split(world);
borrow mut io as &!i in { greet(i); }

steps.cap: This time greet’s signature claims it does nothing: its effect row is [].
split(world), then the unused four are released.
io is lent to greet, which writes with it.
Effect rows are exact: performing io_write without declaring it is refused. The row is not a comment.
